questions.prompt: A candidate argues that `malloc` is acceptable on the tick-to-trade path because a tcmalloc thread-cache pop measures 15–30 ns. What is the strongest rebuttal?
options: The distribution has an unbounded tail: cache refill takes a central lock, heap extension is an `mmap` syscall, and each fresh 4 KB page faults at 1–3 μs on first touch.
The fast-path figure is measured single-threaded, and on a multi-core box the thread cache is shared, so every pop under load contends on the same central free list.
The 15–30 ns figure predates KPTI, and post-mitigation kernels charge every `malloc` a mode switch, so the true modern fast path is closer to 250 ns per call.
The fast path is accurate but irrelevant because the compiler cannot inline through `malloc`, so each call costs a register spill set worth several hundred nanoseconds.
questions.explanation: The ban is about the shape of the distribution, not the mean: p50 is fine while p99.99 is catastrophic, because slow paths take a lock, a syscall, and a run of minor faults. The 'shared thread cache' answer sounds right but inverts the design — the thread cache is per-thread, which is precisely why the fast path is lock-free. The KPTI framing is also wrong: `malloc`'s fast path makes no syscall at all.

questions.prompt: A team allocates a 1 GB hot-path arena with a single `new` at startup and still sees multi-microsecond spikes for the first minutes of trading. What is the diagnosis?
options: Allocation is not residency — the pages are unfaulted, so each first touch costs a 1–3 μs minor fault; the fix is `MAP_POPULATE` plus `mlock`.
The arena is larger than L3, so every access is a compulsory cache miss until the hardware prefetcher learns the stride and the spikes disappear on their own.
A 1 GB request bypasses the allocator's size classes and goes to `brk`, so each subsequent access re-enters the kernel to extend the break by one page.
The arena is not aligned to a huge-page boundary, so the kernel silently splits it and charges a TLB shootdown on every access that crosses a 2 MB region.
questions.explanation: Reserving address space says nothing about physical residency: Linux populates lazily, so the first touch of each page traps, and only prefaulting plus `mlock` makes residency guaranteed and durable. The cache-miss answer is the most tempting because it is true that a cold arena misses, but an L3 miss is ~80 ns, not microseconds, and it cannot produce the observed magnitude. `brk` is not re-entered per access either — the fault is the page-fault handler, not a repeated syscall.

questions.prompt: A config thread `mmap`s and `memset`s the hot arena on behalf of the trading thread, which later runs pinned to a different socket. What does the chapter say this costs?
options: Linux first-touch assigns each physical page to the touching thread's NUMA node, so the trading thread pays roughly 50 ns extra per access permanently.
The memory is correct but cold, so the trading thread pays one compulsory miss per line and then runs at full speed once the working set is resident.
The kernel migrates the pages automatically on the first remote access via AutoNUMA, so the cost is a one-time page-migration burst of a few milliseconds.
The `memset` faults the pages in on the wrong node, so `mlock` silently fails and the pages remain eligible for reclaim under memory pressure.
questions.explanation: First-touch policy binds the physical page to the node of whichever thread wrote it first, so prefaulting on a foreign thread makes every subsequent hot access a remote one — a permanent tax rather than a warm-up cost. The 'cold but then fine' answer is the tempting one because it correctly describes cache behaviour, but NUMA placement is not fixed by warming: DRAM latency stays ~130 ns instead of ~80 ns forever. `mlock` succeeds regardless of node, so that variant is false too.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter insist on explicit `hugetlbfs`/`MAP_HUGETLB` pages rather than transparent huge pages for a hot-path arena?
options: THP's `khugepaged` compaction produces multi-millisecond stalls, the classic cause of p99.99 spikes every few minutes.
THP only backs file-backed mappings, so an anonymous hot-path arena never receives 2 MB pages regardless of the system setting.
THP pages cannot be locked with `mlock`, so a transparently promoted arena remains eligible for reclaim under memory pressure.
THP uses 4 MB pages on x86-64, which do not match the L2 TLB's entry format and therefore raise rather than lower TLB pressure.
questions.explanation: Both mechanisms reduce TLB pressure, so the deciding factor is jitter: the kernel's background compaction thread stalls the process at unpredictable moments, which is exactly the tail behaviour the chapter forbids. The claim that THP is file-backed only is backwards — THP historically applies to anonymous memory, which is what an arena is. The page-size claim is also wrong; x86-64 huge pages are 2 MB (or 1 GB), and a 1 GB working set needs 512 of them versus 262,144 4 KB entries.

questions.prompt: Why do many low-latency firms disable Turbo Boost even though it raises single-core frequency above base?
options: Turbo is opportunistic — the achievable bin varies with active core count, package temperature, and instruction mix, and can drop mid-burst, converting speed into jitter.
Turbo transitions require a 10–50 μs frequency change on every entry and exit, so a core that boosts and drops repeatedly spends most of a burst in transition.
Turbo is incompatible with `isolcpus`, because the governor needs load-balancer statistics that isolated cores no longer report to the kernel.
Turbo raises the core's C-state exit latency into the C6 range, so a boosted core takes far longer to respond to the first packet after idling.
questions.explanation: The trade is a lower mean for a constant one: because the sustainable boost bin depends on conditions outside your control and can change mid-burst, Turbo makes the clock a source of jitter, and the chapter's thesis is that predictability beats speed at the tail. The transition-cost answer is the closest miss — the 10–50 μs figure is real, but the chapter attaches it to P-state governor transitions generally, and the stated objection to Turbo is variability of the achievable frequency. Turbo neither conflicts with `isolcpus` nor alters C-state exit latency.

questions.prompt: A pool's free list is changed from LIFO to FIFO so that slots 'rotate evenly and wear uniformly'. What is the measured effect on a pool larger than L2?
options: Each acquire cycles to the coldest slot and guarantees a cache miss, typically 40–80 ns worse per acquire than LIFO.
Acquire cost is unchanged since both are an index load and a counter update, but release becomes a two-pointer update instead of one.
Throughput improves because the hardware prefetcher recognizes the sequential sweep through the slot array and hides the miss latency.
The change is neutral for latency but doubles the free list's memory footprint, since FIFO needs both a head and a tail index.
questions.explanation: LIFO hands back the most recently freed slot, which is still resident in L1/L2; FIFO walks the entire pool before reusing anything, so once the pool exceeds L2 every acquire touches a cold line. The prefetcher answer is the seductive one — the sweep really is sequential — but the miss is on the payload slot the caller is about to write, and the miss is incurred at acquire time regardless of what a prefetcher eventually learns. The arithmetic cost of the counter update is not what distinguishes the two.

questions.prompt: The chapter recommends handing out dense `uint32_t` indices from a pool rather than `T*`. Which claim about that choice is correct?
options: The handle is half a pointer's size, stays valid across processes in shared memory, and doubles as the correlation-table key.
The handle removes the pointer arithmetic from `release`, since the index is stored directly rather than recovered by subtraction.
The handle lets the pool grow by reallocating the slot array, because indices survive a move where raw pointers would dangle.
The handle allows the compiler to prove non-aliasing between slots, so accesses through two different indices can be reordered freely.
questions.explanation: The stated benefits are footprint (32 bits instead of 64 in hot structures), shared-memory stability, and reuse as the order-correlation key. The 'lets the pool grow' answer is the plausible trap: it is a real property of indices in general, but a hot-path pool has fixed compile-time capacity and never reallocates, so it is not the reason given. `release` still computes `p - slots_`, and indices grant the compiler no aliasing guarantee.

questions.prompt: A feed handler allocates event objects from its pool and a journal-writer thread on another core frees them. What structure does the chapter prescribe?
options: Keep the pool per-thread and add an SPSC return ring so the freeing thread pushes indices back for the owner to drain lazily.
Promote the pool to a lock-free multi-producer free list using a tagged CAS loop so either thread can push and pop safely.
Give the journal writer its own pool and have the feed handler copy each event across, so neither pool is ever touched by two threads.
Guard the shared free list with an uncontended spinlock, which costs a single CAS and is affordable at roughly 20 ns per operation.
questions.explanation: The prescription is per-thread pools plus an SPSC return ring, so neither side executes an atomic RMW beyond the ring's single sequence counter. The multi-producer CAS answer is exactly the design error the chapter names: it reintroduces an atomic into acquire and brings an ABA hazard with it. The copy-across variant does avoid sharing but pays a full event copy per message, which the chapter's single-writer plus return-ring pattern exists to avoid.

questions.prompt: A spin loop is rewritten to call `recvfrom()` on a non-blocking socket every iteration instead of blocking on `epoll_wait`. How does the chapter judge this?
options: Worse than blocking: it pays a syscall on every iteration and still burns the whole core, so it loses on both counts.
Better than blocking on latency but worse on power, since the wakeup path is gone while the core now runs at 100% duty.
Equivalent to blocking, because a non-blocking `recvfrom` that finds no data returns from the vDSO without a mode switch.
Better than kernel bypass for small deployments, since it keeps the kernel's checksum and reassembly work off the critical path.
questions.explanation: Spinning only pays off when the steady state contains no syscall, which requires kernel bypass or busy-poll socket options; a `recvfrom` per iteration keeps the 1–3 μs mode-switch cost and adds the cost of a fully consumed core. The 'better on latency, worse on power' answer is the tempting half-truth — it credits the design with removing the wakeup while ignoring that a syscall per iteration reinstates a comparable cost. `recvfrom` is a genuine syscall, not a vDSO call.

questions.prompt: Where does the chapter say `_mm_pause()` belongs, and where does it say to omit it?
options: Use it in a contention spin waiting on another core's write; omit it when polling a NIC descriptor or SPSC ring, where it only adds latency.
Use it in any loop that runs more than a few iterations; omit it only when the spinning core has its SMT sibling disabled in BIOS.
Use it when polling a NIC descriptor to give DMA time to land; omit it in contention spins, where it delays observing the other core's store.
Use it whenever the loop body contains an atomic load; omit it when the loop reads only plain non-atomic memory locations.
questions.explanation: In a contention spin, `PAUSE` reduces memory-order-violation machine clears and stops the thread from starving its SMT sibling; in a polling loop against a NIC or ring there is no such violation to avoid, so the ~35-cycle delay is pure added latency. The inverted variant is the strongest distractor because it invents a sensible-sounding rationale — giving DMA time to land — but nothing about `PAUSE` accelerates a DMA write, and delaying the poll only delays detection.

questions.prompt: Which cost of busy-spinning does the chapter classify as desirable rather than as a drawback to be mitigated?
options: Keeping the package out of deep C-states, since a core that never idles never pays a C-state exit latency.
Consuming a whole core, since a dedicated core guarantees the thread never competes for front-end bandwidth.
Drawing roughly 10–25 W per core, since the sustained thermal load keeps the die at a stable operating temperature.
Removing fairness entirely, since a thread that never yields cannot be preempted by the kernel's load balancer.
questions.explanation: The chapter's cost table marks the frequency and C-state effect as deliberate — a busy core stays out of deep idle states, which is the strongest single argument for spinning given C6 exit latencies up to 150 μs. The 'whole core is a feature' answer is the tempting one, but the chapter lists core consumption squarely as a cost requiring capacity planning; SMT bandwidth is a separate concern addressed by isolating siblings. Power and lack of fairness are also listed as costs needing mitigation.

questions.prompt: A host boots with `isolcpus=2-7` and the trading thread is pinned to core 4, yet `cyclictest` shows a recurring 1–3 μs interference roughly a thousand times a second. What is missing?
options: `nohz_full` — `isolcpus` removes the core from load balancing but the 1000 Hz scheduler tick still fires on it.
`SCHED_FIFO` — under `SCHED_OTHER` the CFS scheduler still preempts the thread at each of its periodic quantum boundaries.
`mlockall` — the recurring cost is the kernel's page reclaim scanner touching the thread's resident pages once per millisecond.
A second pinned thread — `isolcpus` cores are parked at low frequency until at least two runnable tasks are present on them.
questions.explanation: The thousand-per-second cadence is the signature of the `CONFIG_HZ=1000` scheduler tick, which `isolcpus` does not stop; `nohz_full` does, provided exactly one runnable task is on the core. The `SCHED_FIFO` answer is the most tempting because scheduling policy is genuinely part of the isolation discussion, but with real `isolcpus` nothing competes, so `SCHED_OTHER` is adequate and policy is only a backstop. Adding a second thread would make things worse, since it re-enables the tick.

questions.prompt: An engineer pins the NIC-facing receive thread to `cpu1` because `cpu0` handles interrupts and `cpu1` 'must be the next core over'. What is wrong?
options: Core numbering follows BIOS enumeration, not topology, so `cpu1` may be `cpu0`'s SMT sibling or on another socket entirely; read `lscpu -e` first.
Interrupt handling always occupies the first two logical CPUs on Linux, so `cpu1` is already reserved and the affinity call will silently fail.
The receive thread must share a physical core with the interrupt handler so the packet arrives in the same L1, so `cpu1` is too far away.
Pinning to a single logical CPU disables `nohz_full` on that core, so the thread should be pinned to a two-core mask instead.
questions.explanation: Logical CPU indices are assigned by firmware enumeration and carry no topological meaning, so hardcoding them can silently place the RX thread on a sibling hyperthread or across a socket from the NIC's PCIe root complex. The 'share a core with the IRQ handler' answer inverts the chapter's rule: interrupts are moved off the isolated core entirely, and the pairing rule is NUMA-node locality to the NIC, not L1 sharing. `nohz_full` requires a single runnable task, not a wider affinity mask.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter say about running the hot thread under `SCHED_FIFO` on a properly isolated core?
options: It is a defensible backstop against a stray process, but a non-yielding spinner at FIFO priority can starve kernel threads and hang a misconfigured host.
It is required, because `isolcpus` only excludes a core from load balancing and `SCHED_OTHER` threads remain preemptible by any other runnable task.
It is forbidden, because real-time priorities disable `nohz_full` on the core and reinstate the periodic tick the isolation was meant to remove.
It is neutral, because the scheduler never runs on an isolated core at all, so the policy field has no observable effect on the thread.
questions.explanation: With genuine isolation `SCHED_OTHER` suffices since nothing competes; FIFO is offered only as insurance, carrying the real hazard that a spin loop which never yields blocks kernel threads that legitimately need the core. The 'it is required' framing is the plausible miss — it correctly notes that `isolcpus` is about load balancing, but on an isolated core there is no competing runnable task for CFS to schedule. Real-time priority does not interact with `nohz_full` in the way the forbidden-variant claims.

questions.prompt: A hot path reads risk limits that a control thread updates a few times a day. `std::shared_mutex` is proposed since reads vastly outnumber writes. Why does the chapter reject it?
options: Acquiring the shared lock writes the lock word, so every reader takes the line exclusively and bounces it; a seqlock reader issues no stores at all.
Reader-writer locks starve the writer under continuous read load, so a limit update could be delayed indefinitely while the hot path keeps reading.
`std::shared_mutex` allocates its reader-count state on first use, so the first hot-path acquisition on each thread reaches the allocator.
Shared locking requires a full sequentially-consistent fence on both acquire and release, costing roughly 100 ns per read on modern x86.
questions.explanation: The decisive property is that shared acquisition is itself a store, so concurrent readers serialize on coherence traffic — which is why `shared_mutex` can be slower than a plain mutex under read-heavy hot-path load, and why a store-free seqlock reader wins. Writer starvation is the strongest distractor: it is a real hazard of some reader-writer designs, but it is a fairness concern about the cold writer, not the hot-path latency argument the chapter makes. `std::shared_mutex` does not allocate per acquisition.

questions.prompt: According to the chapter's avoidance hierarchy, which characterization of the options is accurate?
options: No sharing costs zero and is the default to restructure toward; an SPSC ring hands off in ~20–40 ns; a seqlock read is ~5 ns.
A lock-free MPMC queue costs ~20 ns and is preferred over an SPSC ring because it removes the single-producer restriction for free.
An uncontended mutex costs ~20 ns and is therefore acceptable on the critical path provided contention is measured to be rare.
A relaxed atomic RMW costs ~1 ns and so a shared counter incremented by two hot threads is equivalent to a thread-local one.
questions.explanation: The hierarchy runs from no sharing at zero cost, through SPSC hand-offs at 20–40 ns, to seqlock reads around 5 ns, with mutexes reserved for the cold path. The 'uncontended mutex is affordable' answer is the most tempting because the 20 ns figure is correct — but the rule is categorical precisely because contention is unbounded, costing 2–10 μs to resume and potentially convoying. An MPMC queue costs 40–100 ns under contention, and a relaxed RMW is 7–20 ns, not 1 ns, with cross-core bouncing on top.

questions.prompt: In the chapter's seqlock, why does the reader retry when the sequence counter it read first is odd?
options: An odd counter means the writer is mid-update, so the payload may be torn and any copy taken now must be discarded.
An odd counter means the writer has completed but not yet published, so the payload is stale by exactly one generation.
An odd counter means another reader holds the structure, so retrying preserves the single-reader invariant the seqlock requires.
An odd counter means the payload straddles a cache line, so the reader must retry until the two halves land in the same line.
questions.explanation: The writer increments the counter before and after the payload write, so odd marks an in-progress update whose data cannot be trusted; the reader spins and retries, and the second read of the counter catches any update that started during the copy. The 'complete but unpublished' answer is the closest miss — it describes a plausible publication protocol, but here odd strictly brackets the write itself. Seqlocks impose no single-reader rule; multiple readers are exactly the case they serve.

questions.prompt: A profiler shows a hot thread calling `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` three times per event. Which correction matches the chapter?
options: Each call is ~20–25 ns of vDSO work rather than a syscall; timestamp once with `rdtsc` at ~7 ns and convert to nanoseconds off the hot path.
Each call is a ~250 ns syscall post-KPTI; replace it with a single `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE)`, which is served from a cached kernel value.
Each call is ~20–25 ns but the calls are independent, so the compiler merges them into one; the real fix is to remove the redundant timestamp fields.
Each call is ~7 ns, comparable to `rdtsc`, so the cost is acceptable and the effort belongs on removing the surrounding logging instead.
questions.explanation: For `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` the vDSO maps timekeeping data into userspace, so there is no mode switch — it is a ~20–25 ns function call, acceptable once per event but not three times, and `rdtsc` at ~7 ns with offline conversion is the hot-path pattern. The KPTI-syscall answer is the most tempting because syscall costs really did jump post-2018, but that premise does not apply to a vDSO-served clock. The compiler cannot merge the calls, since each must observe a fresh time value.

questions.prompt: Beyond the direct ~250 ns mode-switch cost, what indirect cost of a syscall does the chapter say microbenchmarks of the syscall itself never capture?
options: It pollutes L1i, L1d, and the branch predictors, so the next few hundred instructions of your own code run measurably slower.
It forces the thread onto the kernel stack, which is not in the thread's NUMA-local memory, so the return path pays a remote access.
It resets the core's frequency governor sample window, so a burst of syscalls prevents the core from reaching its Turbo bin.
It flushes the store buffer, so all pending stores retire synchronously and the following stores stall until the buffer refills.
questions.explanation: The chapter's point is that a syscall evicts your instruction and data footprint and disturbs the predictors, so the slowdown extends past the return into your own code — invisible to a loop that measures only the syscall. The frequency answer is plausible-sounding but conflates the power-state material of a later section with the mode-switch cost, and syscall bursts are not what keeps a busy core out of Turbo. Store-buffer drain is not the mechanism described.

questions.prompt: A hot path is audited and found to be free of `write`, `sendto`, and `epoll_wait`, yet `perf trace` shows occasional microsecond stalls on the first call into a shared library. What is the cause and fix?
options: Lazy PLT binding resolves the symbol through the dynamic loader on first call; fix with `LD_BIND_NOW=1`/`-Wl,-z,now` or static linking.
The shared library's text pages are demand-paged from disk on first call; fix by copying the library into tmpfs so the pages are memory-backed.
The loader takes a global lock around every cross-library call; fix by marking the hot symbols `__attribute__((visibility("hidden")))` in the caller.
The PLT indirection defeats the branch-target buffer on every call; fix by hoisting the call into a function pointer cached at startup.
questions.explanation: The chapter lists lazy PLT binding among the hidden syscalls: the first call to each shared-library function runs a dynamic-loader resolution costing microseconds, removed by eager binding or static linking. The demand-paging answer is the strongest distractor because first-touch faults on library text are a real phenomenon — but it does not explain a per-symbol first-call cost, and it is not the mechanism named. The loader does not lock every cross-library call, and a warm PLT entry predicts fine.

questions.prompt: In the chapter's deferred-formatting logger, why is `const char* fmt` stored rather than the format text itself?
options: A string literal has static storage duration, so the pointer stays valid for the consumer and a 40-byte copy becomes 8 bytes.
The pointer value is stable across process restarts, so an offline decoder can resolve it against the binary's `.rodata` section.
Storing the pointer lets the consumer mutate the format in place when a field turns out to need a wider conversion specifier.
The pointer is naturally aligned, so the record's argument array following it needs no padding to reach 8-byte alignment.
questions.explanation: Static storage duration is what makes the deferral safe, and it shrinks the record dramatically since only 8 bytes are captured on the hot side. The offline-decoder answer is the tempting near-miss: the chapter does describe an offline decoder, but for the further refinement where each call site gets a compile-time integer ID and a build-time dictionary — raw pointer values are not stable across restarts under ASLR. Alignment is incidental, not the reason.

questions.prompt: A developer calls `log_hot("filled %s", sym.c_str())` where `sym` is a `std::string` local. What goes wrong, and what is the prescribed guard?
options: The pointer dangles before the consumer formats it, producing garbage or a crash later in another thread; constrain the API with `static_assert` to reject non-static pointers.
The `c_str()` call itself allocates when the string is short, so the hot side reaches the allocator; take a `std::string_view` parameter to avoid the conversion cost.
The consumer copies the string bytes into the ring, so the record exceeds its fixed 48-byte size and the ring silently truncates the trailing arguments.
The pointer is fine because the ring is drained within microseconds, but the string's heap page may not be locked, so formatting can take a minor fault.
questions.explanation: Deferred formatting means the consumer dereferences the pointer long after the local has died, and the failure surfaces minutes later on a different thread with no link to the original code — so the API must reject non-static pointers at compile time. The 'drained within microseconds' answer is the most seductive because it sounds like a bounded window, but the ring's drain latency is not a lifetime guarantee and the local dies at scope exit regardless. `c_str()` does not allocate, and the record never copies the characters.

questions.prompt: The logging ring is full during a burst. Which behaviour does the chapter require?
options: Drop the record, increment a counter, and export that counter as a first-class metric — never block and never allocate.
Block the producer briefly so the consumer can catch up, since losing records during a burst destroys the evidence you most need.
Grow the ring geometrically for the duration of the burst and shrink it back once the consumer drains, keeping every record.
Overwrite the oldest unread record, since the newest events carry the most diagnostic value during an ongoing incident.
questions.explanation: The producer must be bounded, non-blocking, and non-allocating, so dropping is the only admissible outcome — but silent dropping is forbidden, hence the exported drop counter. The 'block briefly' answer is the strongest distractor because its motivation is real: bursts are when records matter most. Yet blocking puts the consumer's I/O tail directly on the hot path, which is exactly what the split architecture exists to prevent. Growing the ring reintroduces allocation.

questions.prompt: A team replaces a perfectly-predicted runtime `if (venue == Nasdaq)` in the encode path with `if constexpr` under a `Venue` template parameter and is surprised the branch removal buys nothing. Where does the real win come from?
options: The untaken encoder is never instantiated, so the hot loop's I-cache footprint shrinks, and the known constant enables downstream folding and unrolling.
The template parameter forces the compiler to inline the encoder, and inlining alone removes the call overhead that dominated the measurement.
`if constexpr` moves the comparison into the linker's layout phase, so the hot path's instructions become contiguous and prefetch as one stream.
The template instantiation gives each venue its own branch-predictor history slot, so the predictor no longer aliases the two venues' outcomes.
questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that branch elimination is worth roughly nothing for a well-predicted branch; the gains are I-cache footprint from dropping the dead code, constant propagation enabling bounds-check folding and unrolling, removed loads, and `%` becoming `&`. The inlining answer is tempting because inlining is a genuine template benefit, but a direct call to `encode_ouch` was already inlinable without the template. `if constexpr` is a compile-time construct, not a linker layout mechanism.

questions.prompt: The venue is only known at runtime from configuration. How does the chapter reconcile that with compile-time specialization?
options: Dispatch once at the edge — a single switch at startup or the top of the loop selects a monomorphic instantiation, costing one indirect call per connection.
Specialize on every venue and select with a function-pointer table indexed per message, which costs one predictable indirect call and keeps bodies inlined.
Abandon specialization for the encode step and keep it only for capacity constants, since a runtime venue makes template instantiation impossible.
Instantiate all venues and rely on the compiler's speculative devirtualization to pick the hot one, guarded by a runtime type check it can fold away.
questions.explanation: The resolution is one dispatch at the boundary followed by a fully monomorphic run loop, so the indirect call is paid per connection rather than per message. The per-message function-pointer table is the plausible trap: it is true that such a call predicts well, but a function pointer remains an inlining barrier, so the specialized bodies stop folding into the caller and the main benefit is lost. Runtime configuration does not make instantiation impossible — the switch selects among instantiations.

questions.prompt: A reviewer asks for `[[likely]]` annotations throughout the hot path 'so the predictor learns the right direction'. What is the accurate correction?
options: The attributes affect code layout only — likely path as fall-through, cold path out of line; they do not train the predictor, and PGO or BOLT does this better automatically.
The attributes emit branch-hint prefixes that modern x86 front-ends honour on first execution, so they help only until the predictor has warmed up.
The attributes are advisory and ignored at `-O2`, so they change nothing at all; only `__builtin_expect` has any effect on generated code.
The attributes bias the predictor's initial state, so they are valuable exactly for branches taken rarely enough that the predictor never converges.
questions.explanation: Their effect is layout: the likely side falls through and the cold side is pushed out of line, improving I-cache density, and profile-guided optimization plus BOLT do the same job across the whole binary from real data — commonly 5–15% on hot-path trading binaries. The 'biases the predictor's initial state' answer is the most tempting because it sounds like a mechanism, but no such training channel exists. `[[likely]]` is not ignored at `-O2`; it is simply a layout hint rather than a predictor hint.

questions.prompt: A microbenchmark shows a virtual method call is 3–10× slower than the devirtualized equivalent, though the dispatch itself measures only 2–5 ns. What explains the gap?
options: The virtual call is an optimization barrier: the direct version disappears into the caller, enabling folding, vectorization, and no forced spills.
The vptr load misses cache on every call, since the object header is on a different line from the fields the method actually reads.
The indirect call flushes the return-stack buffer, so the return from the virtual method mispredicts and costs an additional pipeline refill.
The vtable lives in a shared read-only page, so each call takes a TLB entry that competes with the hot path's data working set.
questions.explanation: The dispatch cost is small; the loss is that the compiler cannot inline through the indirect call, so it cannot constant-fold, cannot vectorize across it, must assume a memory clobber, and must spill caller-saved registers — while the direct call vanishes entirely into the caller. The vptr-miss answer is the strongest distractor: cache misses on the header are real in scattered object graphs, but a tight benchmark loop keeps the object hot, and the ratio persists anyway. The RSB is not disturbed by an ordinary indirect call.

questions.prompt: A feed handler holds `vector<unique_ptr<Handler>>` and calls `->on_message()` per packet. Which restructuring does the chapter identify as the answer interviewers want?
options: Partition into one array per concrete type processed in homogeneous batches, making the call monomorphic and inlinable and the access pattern sequential.
Mark every leaf handler `final` and enable LTO, which lets the compiler devirtualize the container's call site into a direct, inlinable call.
Replace `unique_ptr` with `std::function` holding a captureless lambda per handler, removing the vptr load from the per-packet dispatch.
Sort the vector by handler address at startup so the indirect targets are contiguous and the branch-target buffer predicts them reliably.
questions.explanation: Data-oriented partitioning fixes two problems at once: the call becomes monomorphic and inlines, and the objects are contiguous rather than scattered, so the per-element cache miss disappears. Marking leaves `final` plus LTO is the closest miss — the chapter genuinely calls `final` the cheapest devirtualization win, but it cannot help a call site whose static type is the polymorphic base and whose container legitimately holds several types. `std::function` is disqualified outright as an allocating inlining barrier.

questions.prompt: A quoting gateway rebuilds its full 28-byte order message field by field on every price update. What does the chapter recommend, and what does it claim it buys?
options: Keep one pre-populated buffer per instrument and overwrite only price, quantity, and `ClOrdID`, cutting an encode from around 30 stores to about 6.
Serialize into a thread-local `std::vector<std::byte>` reserved at startup, so the stores are identical but the destination is guaranteed warm and resident.
Compute the whole message in registers and issue one 32-byte AVX store, so the encode becomes a single instruction against the transmit buffer.
Cache the last message and `memcmp` it against the new one, sending nothing when they match, which removes most encodes entirely during quiet periods.
questions.explanation: Session, account, sender and header fields are invariant, so writing them once at startup into a per-instrument warm buffer leaves the hot path editing two or three fields — the chapter's ~30-stores-to-~6 figure, with encode times of a handful of nanoseconds. The AVX answer is the tempting one because a single wide store sounds optimal, but the chapter warns that incidental wide vector instructions trigger frequency licensing and downclock the core. A vector destination is still a full re-encode.

questions.prompt: A parser takes the address of a member inside a `#pragma pack(1)` foreign-format struct and passes it to a helper. What is the chapter's verdict?
options: Taking the address of a packed member is undefined behaviour and faults on strict-alignment targets; `memcpy` the field out instead.
It is safe on x86-64 because unaligned loads are supported in hardware, and the compiler inserts the split accesses where alignment demands it.
It is safe provided the struct itself is allocated with `alignas(64)`, since the outer alignment then guarantees every member is naturally aligned.
It is a portability concern only, so it should be resolved by a `static_assert` on `offsetof` rather than by changing how the field is read.
questions.explanation: A pointer to a packed member may be misaligned for its type, which is UB in C++ and traps on strict-alignment targets — hence `-Waddress-of-packed-member` and the advice to `memcpy` fields out of foreign formats. The x86-64 answer is the most tempting because hardware really does tolerate unaligned loads, but tolerance at the ISA level does not make the language construct defined, and the code stops working the moment it is built for ARM. Aligning the outer struct cannot fix interior packing.

questions.prompt: A fixed-layout decode of a small market-data update measures 800 ns instead of the expected 5–20 ns. Which explanation is consistent with the chapter?
options: A `std::string` or `snprintf` crept into the path, or the decode is a tag-based parse loop, or the destination buffer is unaligned or cold.
The struct is trivially copyable, so the compiler emits a byte-wise copy loop rather than the wide loads a non-trivial type would permit.
The venue's byte order differs from the host's, and `__builtin_bswap` on each field adds roughly 100 ns per multi-byte member.
The wire-length bounds check before indexing is a mispredicted branch, and at 15–20 cycles per field it dominates a small message's decode.
questions.explanation: The chapter's checklist for a decode measuring hundreds of nanoseconds names exactly these causes: hidden container or formatting calls, a table-driven tag parse, an unaligned buffer, or a cold destination page. The bounds-check answer is the most tempting because the check is real and mandatory, but it is a compare and a highly predictable branch worth a handful of cycles — and skipping it is how a malformed message becomes an out-of-bounds read. Byte swapping is about one cycle per field, not 100 ns.

questions.prompt: A startup script opens `/dev/cpu_dma_latency`, writes a 32-bit zero, and closes the descriptor. What has it achieved?
options: Nothing — the PM QoS constraint is released when the descriptor closes, so the cores are free to enter deep C-states again.
A permanent system-wide C-state cap, since the value is persisted by the PM QoS subsystem until another writer replaces it.
A cap that applies only to the writing process's cores, since PM QoS constraints are inherited by the thread's CPU affinity mask.
A frequency floor rather than a C-state cap, since a zero-microsecond bound is interpreted by the driver as a request for maximum P-state.
questions.explanation: The constraint lives only as long as the open file description; closing it withdraws the request, which is why the chapter calls a held-open descriptor the detail that distinguishes candidates who have actually done the work. The 'permanent system-wide cap' answer is the natural assumption from the write-once-and-forget model of other `/proc` and `/sys` knobs, but PM QoS is deliberately fd-scoped. The interface caps idle-state exit latency, not frequency, and it is global rather than per-affinity.
